name: יִגְאָל
gloss: he redeems; or may he redeem
summary: Borne by three men: Igal son of Joseph, the spy sent from the tribe of Issachar to search out Canaan (Num 13:7); Igal son of Nathan of Zobah, one of David's mighty men (2Sa 23:36); and Igal son of Shemaiah, a descendant of Zerubbabel after the exile (1Ch 3:22). The name is the qal imperfect of גָּאַל, the same form as Boaz's “let him redeem” (Rut 3:13): “he redeems”, with God the unspoken subject, as in Yahweh's name “Redeemer” (Isa 44:6). Scripture does not explain it.

evidence.note: “For the tribe of Issachar, יִגְאָל son of Joseph.”
“יִגְאָל son of Nathan of Zobah”, among David's mighty men.
“The sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, וְיִגְאָל, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat.”
“If he will redeem you, good, יִגְאָל”: the same form, “let him redeem”.
“Yahweh, the King of Israel, and his redeemer.”

note: Takes c.ac.ad (3 tokens). j.aj.af, a zero-token verb cross-reference spelled יִגְאָל, is left unassigned. The Hebrew of 2Sa 23:36 has יִגְאָל; the parallel list in 1Ch 11:38 has יוֹאֵל, brother of Nathan, the Septuagint's ιωηλ at one of the three; whether these are one man is not settled here. The name's subject (God) is assumed from the pattern of names such as יִשְׁמָעֵאל; no verse gives it.
